cim: Undergraduate research shapes this future physician
cim_eredeti: Undergraduate research shapes this future physician
szoveg_eredeti:
One question underlies Carolina senior Suhan Asaigoli’s computational medicine research: “How can I use computer science in the lab to diagnose and treat disorders and help patients?”

Asaigoli, a neuroscience major in the UNC College of Arts and Sciences, has been seeking answers to this as far back as his middle school days.

As a college-bound student at Enloe High School in Raleigh, Asaigoli had his eye on the public research powerhouse in Chapel Hill known for its health affairs expertise. His acceptance here included admission to Carolina’s Accelerated Research program, which shows Tar Heels the research ropes early and connects them with valuable resources.

“It was a really gratifying experience to feel like there was something I wrote in my application that indicated I had some potential to be able to do research and make an impact that way here at Carolina,” said Asaigoli, a Morehead-Cain scholar who plans to become a physician.

In his first semester at Carolina, Asaigoli was already conducting independent research, using computer science to analyze publicly available health and biomedical data.

But Asaigoli, admittedly “picky” about his research focus, also wanted to apply his skills in just the right Carolina lab, so he turned to Bob Pleasants, director of the Office of Undergraduate Research and a leader in the Accelerated Research program.

Pleasants guided Asaigoli on approaching researchers at a symposium hosted by the UNC School of Medicine’s radiology department. Once there, Asaigoli met Dr. Yueh Lee.

“I think you’re doing pretty decent work on your own here. We should get you plugged in,” Lee told him.

Three years later, Asaigoli remains a key member of the Lee Lab, where he’s advanced his machine learning and artificial intelligence research. With Lee and the rest of his lab collaborators, Asaigoli uses those technologies to better identify markers and measurements of neurodegenerative diseases on MRIs and CT scans.

One of Asaigoli’s earliest projects focused on using AI to measure brain structure and detect abnormal fluid buildup to get earlier diagnoses of hydrocephalus.

“You have a disease, you have a certain type of imaging that’s applicable to it, and you use computer science to try to speed up or make more accurate the way we diagnose,” Asaigoli said.

The same approach applies to Asaigoli’s honors thesis on whether AI can perform an accurate blood flow analysis with a CT scan of the brain after a stroke, enabling better and faster clinical decision-making.

Asaigoli also wants his research to lead to the most practical and accessible healthcare solutions. While an MRI scan is considered the gold standard for brain imaging, a CT scan is the “best form of imaging that can be done cheaply and quickly” when a person arrives at the emergency department with a suspected stroke, according to Asaigoli. That’s why he wanted to target improving the form of imaging most often used immediately after a health emergency.

“The fact that it hasn’t necessarily been tackled before is really exciting,” Asaigoli said.

Suhan Asaigoli works in the Shawn Gomez Lab in the Mary Ellen Jones Building on the campus of UNC-Chapel Hill. The senior and Morehead-Cain scholar also works in the lab of Dr. Yueh Lee. (Jon Gardiner/UNC-Chapel Hill)

The Lee Lab isn’t his only research home at Carolina. Asaigoli also works in the Shawn Gomez Lab in the Lampe Joint Department of Biomedical Engineering, researching how illuminating the interactions of kinases, a type of specialized protein, can inform drug development for various disorders.

“Proteins are used for a lot in the body,” Asaigoli said. “They usually have very specific functions that carry out a lot of biological pathways, like how we metabolize energy and clean up our own cells.”

Asaigoli also serves as an OUR research ambassador, helping fellow students home in on the right type of research and find labs aligned with their interests. He wants them to know there’s enough research opportunities for them all.

While at Carolina, Asaigoli has also developed an interest in large-scale public health issues that influence disease and overall health. He’s now thinking about how the technology he uses in the lab can be used to tackle structural problems like food deserts or people living far away from a doctor’s office.

It’s too early for Asaigoli to know what specific type of medicine he might one day practice. But he knows his research experiences as a Tar Heel will guide him.

“I’ll be a physician asking questions and trying to make an impact through the research skills that I built up here at Carolina,” he said.
